title: Digital Asset Market Clarity Act of 2025
official_title: To provide for a system of regulation of the offer and sale of digital commodities by the Securities and Exchange Commission and the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, and for other purposes.
summary: The Digital Asset Market Clarity Act creates a legal framework for digital commodities — digital assets whose value comes from blockchain use — by splitting oversight between the SEC and the CFTC. The CFTC gets exclusive authority over spot and cash markets for digital commodities traded on registered exchanges, while the SEC handles token offerings and regulates broker-dealers who trade digital assets on alternative trading systems. A separate Title VI, the Anti-CBDC Surveillance State Act, bars the Federal Reserve banks from offering products or services directly to individuals and from issuing a central bank digital currency, and bars the Federal Reserve from using a CBDC to conduct monetary policy.
brief: Splits regulation of digital commodities between the CFTC (spot markets and exchanges) and the SEC (token offerings and broker-dealers), and creates a certification path for blockchains to move from SEC oversight to CFTC jurisdiction once they become decentralized, and adds a Title VI barring the Federal Reserve from issuing or using a central bank digital currency.

top_lines.headline: CFTC Gets Exclusive Spot Market Jurisdiction
subs: CFTC has exclusive jurisdiction over spot and cash market transactions in digital commodities on registered entities or by entities required to register with the CFTC

Any trading facility offering a cash or spot market in at least one digital commodity must register as a digital commodity exchange, unless it handles only de minimis trading or serves only a single state

Digital commodity brokers and dealers must also register with the CFTC, which must adopt an expedited registration process within 180 days of enactment; once that process is adopted, operators must register (entering provisional status) or stop acting after a 90-day window

top_lines.headline: Blockchain Maturity Determines Regulator
subs: Issuers may certify their blockchain as a mature blockchain system — not controlled by any person or group — to the SEC; certification takes effect 60 days after filing unless the SEC objects
The SEC may stay a certification for up to an additional 120 days for novel or complex issues; rebutted certifications cannot be refiled for 90 days

Token issuers with blockchains not yet mature may raise up to $50M in a 12-month period under an SEC exemption, provided the blockchain is on track to mature within four years of first sale and no single purchaser acquires more than 10% of outstanding units

top_lines.headline: Insider Resale Restrictions Before Maturity
subs: Related persons (1%+ holders, promoters, senior employees within prior 6 months) and affiliated persons (5%+ holders, founders, directors within prior 12 months) face resale limits before blockchain maturity

Insiders must hold units at least 12 months from delivery before selling; the per-12-month resale cap is set by SEC rule at no less than 5% and no more than 20% of units acquired directly from the issuer
Total insider sales prior to maturity certification are capped by SEC rule at no less than 30% and no more than 50% of units acquired directly from the issuer

top_lines.headline: DeFi Activities Exempt from Registration
subs: Operating a node or oracle service, providing a read-only blockchain user interface, developing or distributing a blockchain system or a decentralized-finance trading protocol, operating or participating in a liquidity pool, and developing or distributing non-custodial wallet software are all exempt from SEC registration
A parallel CFTC exemption under Title IV covers the same six categories of decentralized finance activity
Anti-fraud and anti-manipulation authority of both the SEC and CFTC still applies to exempt decentralized finance activities

top_lines.headline: Anti-CBDC Prohibitions Added (Title VI)
subs: Federal Reserve banks may not offer financial products or services directly to an individual or maintain an account on behalf of an individual

The Federal Reserve may not issue a central bank digital currency directly, or indirectly through a financial institution or other intermediary, and the Board of Governors may not test, study, develop, create, or implement one
The Board of Governors and the Federal Open Market Committee may not use a central bank digital currency to implement monetary policy

likelihoodReason: Introduced by Rep. J. French Hill (R-AR-2) with 21 cosponsors, the bill passed the House 294-134 on July 17, 2025 — a spread that mechanically required cross-party votes since 294 yeas exceed the Republican conference size. A cloture motion on the motion to proceed was presented in the Senate on August 8, 2026 per the latest recorded action, meaning 60 votes are still needed to overcome a Senate filibuster on the Republican-led measure.

sections.label: Title I — Definitions, Rulemaking, and Provisional Registration

items.main: Defines core terms across three statutes — blockchain, digital commodity, mature blockchain system, decentralized governance system, and permitted payment stablecoin — in the Securities Act of 1933, Securities Exchange Act of 1934, and Commodity Exchange Act.
items.detail: A digital commodity is defined as a digital asset intrinsically linked to a blockchain system whose value is derived from the use of that blockchain, and must not be a security, stablecoin, commodity derivative, banking deposit, or pooled investment vehicle. A mature blockchain system is one not controlled by any person or group of persons under common control. Permitted payment stablecoins are excluded from the definitions of both security and digital commodity.

items.main: Requires joint CFTC-SEC rulemaking to further define key terms, to issue delisting rules, procedures, or guidance within 180 days of enactment, and to issue joint portfolio margining rules within 360 days of enactment.
items.detail: The bill also codifies the right of U.S. individuals to maintain hardware or software wallets and to conduct direct peer-to-peer digital asset transactions for personal lawful purposes with non-financial-institution counterparties, provided the transactions do not involve sanctioned property.

items.main: Requires the CFTC to adopt an expedited registration process within 180 days of enactment for digital commodity exchanges, brokers, and dealers; once that process is adopted, a person may not act as such an intermediary beyond a 90-day window unless registered. Registrants enter provisional status, which lasts until 270 days after the CFTC's final rulemakings take effect. Beginning 30 days after enactment, anyone acting as a digital commodity exchange, broker, or dealer must disclose to customers that it is not registered with or regulated by the CFTC.
items.detail: Provisional registrants must join a registered futures association and comply with its customer protection rules. The CFTC collects filing fees from provisional registrants; fees may only be collected in amounts provided in advance by an appropriations act. Late payment incurs a 5% penalty of the fee due multiplied by the number of consecutive 30-day periods overdue. Excess fees collected in any fiscal year must be refunded pro-rata within 60 days after year end.

items.main: Extends Bank Secrecy Act anti-money laundering obligations to digital commodity brokers, digital commodity dealers, and digital commodity exchanges that permit direct customer access.
items.detail: The Comptroller General must issue a report to Congress within one year of enactment assessing risks from foreign-based centralized intermediaries serving U.S. persons without BSA-equivalent requirements, with regulatory or legislative recommendations.

sections.label: Title II — Offers and Sales of Digital Commodities

items.main: Removes investment contract assets from the definition of investment contract in the Securities Act, Securities Exchange Act, Investment Advisers Act, Investment Company Act, and Securities Investor Protection Act. An investment contract asset is a digital commodity transferable person-to-person without an intermediary.
items.detail: Secondary market sales of a digital commodity by persons other than the issuer or its agents are not treated as sales of the original investment contract. End user distributions — broad, equitable distributions not involving more than a nominal exchange of value, such as mining rewards or staking incentives — are not offers or sales of a security.

items.main: Creates a new SEC exemption for token issuers raising up to $50M (annually inflation-adjusted) in a 12-month period via investment contracts in digital commodities, provided the blockchain is on track to achieve maturity within four years of first sale and no purchaser acquires more than 10% of outstanding units.
items.detail: Issuers relying on the $50M exemption must file an offering statement with the SEC including financial information, source code location, transaction history access, unit supply and release schedule, consensus mechanism description, a blockchain maturity development plan, and ownership disclosures for insiders. The exemption is not available to shell companies, investment companies, or issuers subject to an SEC enforcement order in the prior five years.

items.main: Imposes resale restrictions on digital commodity related persons (1%+ holders or promoters/senior employees within the prior 6 months) and affiliated persons (5%+ holders, founders, or current or former directors within the prior 12 months).
items.detail: Insiders must hold units for at least 12 months from delivery before resale. The SEC sets the resale percentages by rule within 270 days of enactment: in any 12-month period, sales are limited to a percentage set no less than 5% and no greater than 20%, and total sales prior to maturity certification to a percentage set no less than 30% and no greater than 50%, of units acquired directly from the issuer.

items.main: Establishes the blockchain maturity certification process: any issuer, related person, affiliated person, or decentralized governance system may file a certification with the SEC that its blockchain is not controlled by any person or group under common control.
items.detail: A certification takes effect 60 days after filing unless the SEC stays it. The SEC may stay a certification once for up to an additional 120 days for novel or complex issues; a public comment period of at least 30 days may be opened within the initial 60-day window. Rebutted certifications may not be refiled for 90 days. If the SEC rebuts a certification, the filer may appeal within 60 days to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit under de novo review.

sections.label: Title III — Registration for Intermediaries at the SEC

items.main: Removes digital commodities and permitted payment stablecoins from the definition of security across five federal statutes: Securities Act of 1933, Securities Exchange Act of 1934, Investment Advisers Act, Investment Company Act, and SIPA.
items.detail: The SEC retains jurisdiction over digital commodity transactions only when a digital commodity is brokered, traded, or custodied by a registered broker-dealer, through a national securities exchange, or through an alternative trading system. Anti-fraud and anti-manipulation rules under Securities Exchange Act Section 10(b) apply to digital commodity and stablecoin transactions in those circumstances to the same extent they apply to securities transactions.

items.main: Allows SEC-registered broker-dealers and national securities exchanges to trade digital commodities and stablecoins without separate CFTC registration; the SEC has rulemaking authority over such activities.
items.detail: Registered broker-dealers, national securities exchanges, and alternative trading systems may also register with the CFTC as digital commodity intermediaries under new Section 15(p) of the Securities Exchange Act; the SEC must require such dual-registered entities to maintain written conflict-of-interest policies, must exempt them from duplicative requirements, and must enter a memorandum of understanding with the CFTC. Trading platforms may not be precluded from operating under a covered SEC exchange exemption solely because they also trade digital commodities alongside securities.

items.main: Exempts six categories of decentralized finance activity from SEC registration: operating nodes or oracle services, providing read-only blockchain interfaces, developing or distributing blockchain software or DeFi protocols, developing non-custodial wallet software, participating in liquidity pools, and providing computational work or network bandwidth.
items.detail: The exemption does not limit SEC anti-fraud and anti-manipulation authority. Banks, broker-dealers, and trust companies providing digital asset custody may not be required to record custodied assets as liabilities on their balance sheets or to hold regulatory capital against them beyond what is necessary to mitigate operational risk.

sections.label: Title IV — Registration for Digital Commodity Intermediaries at the CFTC

items.main: Grants the CFTC exclusive jurisdiction over spot and cash market transactions in digital commodities on registered entities or by entities registered or required to register with the CFTC, amending Commodity Exchange Act Section 2.
items.detail: The CFTC's new jurisdiction does not extend to stablecoin issuer operations, SEC-regulated securities offerings involving digital assets, or custodial activities by entities regulated by a federal banking agency. Digital commodity brokers may, subject to CFTC requirements, offer margin financing agreements to customers for digital commodity purchases.

items.main: Requires trading facilities offering spot or cash markets in at least one digital commodity to register with the CFTC as digital commodity exchanges, subject to CFTC core principles covering trading rules, risk management, customer protection, recordkeeping, and anti-manipulation obligations.
items.detail: Registered digital commodity exchanges and their affiliates may not trade on the exchange for their own account except for customer-directed transactions, risk management, operational needs, or functional blockchain use, with prior CFTC notice. Exchanges accepting customer funds must join a registered futures association. Digital commodity listing requires a written certification to the CFTC that the asset meets applicable requirements, effective 20 business days after filing unless the CFTC disapproves.

items.main: Defines qualified digital asset custodians as entities supervised for digital asset custody by a federal banking agency, NCUA, CFTC, SEC, state bank supervisor, state credit union supervisor, or appropriate foreign governmental authority, meeting minimum capital, asset protection, recordkeeping, and BSA compliance standards.
items.detail: Before CFTC issues final custody rules, state-licensed trust companies expressly permitted by their state bank supervisor to hold digital assets and meeting the minimum standards are deemed qualified custodians. The CFTC must provide a transition period of at least 2 years for such trust companies after final rules take effect.

items.main: Establishes ongoing blockchain control person restrictions: persons with unilateral authority over a certified mature blockchain, or who direct 20% or more of voting rights on that blockchain, must file notice with the CFTC and comply with CFTC-set disclosure and sales restriction rules before selling digital commodity units.
items.detail: The same six categories of decentralized finance activity that are exempt from SEC registration under Title III are also exempt from CFTC registration under Title IV. CFTC anti-fraud, anti-manipulation, and false reporting enforcement authority still applies to exempt activities.

sections.label: Title V — Innovation and Technology Improvements

items.main: Creates standing fintech-engagement offices at both agencies: the SEC's Strategic Hub for Innovation and Financial Technology (FinHub) and a codified LabCFTC at the CFTC.
items.detail: The SEC must establish the Strategic Hub for Innovation and Financial Technology (FinHub) within 180 days of enactment, drawing members from the Divisions of Trading and Markets, Corporate Finance, and Investment Management. FinHub must report annually to the Commission by October 31 of each year after 2025. A parallel provision codifies LabCFTC within the CFTC.

items.main: Requires a series of digital-asset studies under different lead agencies: the CFTC and SEC jointly on decentralized finance (Sec. 504), financial literacy among digital commodity holders (Sec. 506), and financial market infrastructure improvements (Sec. 507); the Treasury Secretary on blockchain in payments (Sec. 508), on illicit use of digital assets (Sec. 509, in consultation with the CFTC and SEC), and on foreign adversary participation (Sec. 511(a), in consultation with the CFTC and SEC); and the Comptroller General (GAO) on non-fungible tokens (Sec. 505), on certain centralized intermediaries primarily located in foreign jurisdictions (Sec. 510, in consultation with the Treasury), on decentralized finance (a separate GAO leg in Sec. 504(d)), and on foreign adversary participation (a separate GAO leg in Sec. 511(b)).
items.detail: The Treasury-led foreign adversary participation study (Sec. 511(a)) must identify digital commodity registrants owned by governments of foreign adversaries, determine whether foreign adversary governments are collecting trading data about U.S. persons in the digital commodity markets, and evaluate whether registrants' proprietary intellectual property is being misused or stolen by those governments.

sections.label: Title VI — Anti-CBDC Surveillance State Act

items.main: Amends the Federal Reserve Act to bar Federal Reserve banks from offering financial products or services directly to an individual, maintaining an account on behalf of an individual, or issuing a central bank digital currency (or any substantially similar digital asset) directly or indirectly through a financial institution or intermediary.
items.detail: The Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System may not test, study, develop, create, or implement a central bank digital currency, and neither the Board nor the Federal Open Market Committee may use one to implement monetary policy. An exception preserves any open, permissionless, and private dollar-denominated currency that fully preserves the privacy protections of physical U.S. coins and currency. A sense of Congress states the Federal Reserve does not currently have authority to issue a CBDC absent a grant from Congress.

underreported.summary: The bill codifies the right of U.S. individuals to maintain hardware or software wallets and to engage in direct peer-to-peer digital asset transactions for their own lawful purposes with non-financial-institution counterparties, provided the transactions do not involve sanctioned property.
underreported.why_unreported: Coverage focuses on the exchange registration and SEC-CFTC jurisdiction split. This provision limits federal agencies' ability to restrict individual self-custody and peer-to-peer transactions — a direct response to concerns about non-custodial wallet software regulation — but is embedded in the rulemaking section of Title I.

underreported.summary: Prohibits the SEC, federal banking agencies, and the NCUA from requiring banks, broker-dealers, or trust companies providing digital asset custody to record custodied assets as liabilities on their balance sheets or to hold regulatory capital against them beyond what is needed for operational risk.
underreported.why_unreported: This changes bank accounting and capital treatment for digital asset custody arrangements — a banking regulatory question separate from the market-structure framework the bill is primarily described as creating.

underreported.section: Section 411 — Control Person Restrictions on Mature Blockchains
underreported.summary: Even after a blockchain achieves certified maturity, persons who retain unilateral authority over the blockchain or who direct 20% or more of its voting rights must file notice with the CFTC and comply with CFTC-set disclosure and sales restriction rules before selling digital commodity units.
underreported.why_unreported: The maturity certification is widely described as a clean transition from SEC to CFTC jurisdiction, but this section imposes ongoing CFTC-enforced obligations on control persons even after the SEC oversight period ends — a continuing restriction that persists past maturity.

gaps: The bill requires the CFTC to expand into spot digital commodity market regulation but Section 410 provides only a fee-collection mechanism; fees may be collected only in amounts provided in advance by a separate appropriations act, leaving the CFTC's new mandate unfunded until Congress appropriates separately.

The bill defines mature blockchain system as one not controlled by any person or group of persons under common control, but does not specify quantitative thresholds for what constitutes control; the SEC must rebut or accept self-certifications within 60 days using this qualitative standard.

The bill exempts decentralized finance activities from registration but does not define the point at which a protocol becomes sufficiently centralized to lose the exemption; this boundary must be established through joint CFTC-SEC rulemaking.

The bill's own stated purpose covers protection of investors in digital commodities but does not establish any compensation or insurance fund analogous to SIPC for customers of digital commodity exchanges that fail or are defrauded.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Lynch
featured_quotes.text: I believe this misguided legislation will have devastating impacts on our financial stability, national security, and investor protection. While my Republican friends claim that this bill will regulate crypto market structure, in reality, it eviscerates the longstanding history of investor protections that have made our markets the envy of the world. Most importantly, this bill, this push for crypto, will not end well for the U.S. taxpayer.

featured_quotes.name: Mr. Emmer
featured_quotes.text: the United States stands at the forefront of the next digital renaissance, a transformative shift toward a decentralized peer-to-peer digital economy. For many years, innovators and investors were forced to operate in a legal gray zone while agencies jostled for regulatory superiority over the digital asset ecosystem, leaving blockchain developers to pack up and move abroad.

added: CFTC exclusive jurisdiction over spot and cash market transactions in digital commodities on registered entities
Mandatory CFTC registration for digital commodity exchanges, brokers, and dealers; 180-day provisional registration window for existing operators
Blockchain maturity certification process: 60-day SEC review, up to 120-day stay extension, 90-day resubmission bar after rebuttal, D.C. Circuit appeal right with de novo review
SEC exemption for investment contract offerings in digital commodities up to $50M (inflation-adjusted) per 12-month period for issuers on a path to blockchain maturity within four years

Insider resale restrictions: 12-month hold plus SEC-set resale caps (5-20% per 12-month period; 30-50% aggregate prior to maturity, set by rule within 270 days), for related persons (1%+) and affiliated persons (5%+)
Qualified digital asset custodian standard for futures commission merchants holding digital assets
Blockchain control person disclosure and sales restriction requirements for persons controlling certified mature blockchains or directing 20%+ of voting rights
Self-custody protection codifying individual rights to maintain wallets and conduct peer-to-peer transactions
Bank Secrecy Act obligations extended to digital commodity brokers, dealers, and direct-access exchanges
DeFi activity exemptions from SEC and CFTC registration covering six categories including node operation, validation, protocol development, and non-custodial wallet software
SEC FinHub committee codified and established within 180 days of enactment; CFTC LabCFTC codified and established upon enactment
GAO study on foreign-based centralized intermediaries serving U.S. persons without BSA-equivalent requirements, due within 1 year of enactment

Anti-CBDC Surveillance State Act (Title VI): bars Federal Reserve banks from offering products or services directly to individuals or issuing a central bank digital currency directly or indirectly, and bars the Federal Reserve from using a CBDC to implement monetary policy

Non-controlling blockchain developers and blockchain-service providers shielded from money-transmitter treatment for publishing software, providing self-custody tools, or maintaining infrastructure (Sec. 109)
Federal Reserve Discretionary Surplus Fund reduced by $15M effective September 30, 2035, as a revenue offset (Sec. 315)

SEC rules (due 270 days after enactment) requiring broker-dealers to give investors written disclosure of how their digital assets would be treated in an insolvency, resolution, or liquidation under Dodd-Frank Title II, SIPA, or Bankruptcy chapter 7 or 11 (Sec. 311)
modified: Securities Act, Securities Exchange Act, Investment Advisers Act, Investment Company Act, SIPA: "investment contract" definition excludes investment contract assets (digital commodities transferable person-to-person without intermediary)
Securities Act, Securities Exchange Act, Investment Advisers Act, Investment Company Act, SIPA: digital commodities and permitted payment stablecoins excluded from definition of security
Commodity Exchange Act Section 1a: digital commodity added as a commodity type; new definitions for digital commodity broker, dealer, exchange, DeFi messaging system, and DeFi trading protocol

Commodity Exchange Act Section 2: CFTC jurisdiction expanded to digital commodity spot markets; CFTC jurisdiction over stablecoin transactions limited to exchange-traded or broker-facilitated contexts
removed: Requirement for banks, broker-dealers, and trust companies to record custodied digital assets as liabilities on balance sheets
Requirement to hold regulatory capital against digital assets held in custody beyond operational risk requirements

added: New Title VI "Anti-CBDC Surveillance State Act" added: bars Federal Reserve banks from offering products/services directly to individuals, from issuing a central bank digital currency directly or indirectly, and from using a CBDC for monetary policy (Secs. 601-605)

New Sec. 109 shields non-controlling blockchain developers and blockchain-service providers from being treated as money transmitters for publishing software, providing self-custody tools, or maintaining infrastructure
New Sec. 311 (broker/dealer) requires written disclosure of how customer digital assets are treated in insolvency/liquidation (Dodd-Frank Title II, SIPA, or Bankruptcy chapters 7/11)
New Sec. 314 educational-material requirement and new Sec. 315 cutting the Fed Discretionary Surplus Fund by $15,000,000 effective September 30, 2035
New Sec. 412 "Other tradable assets" (CEA 4x/6e) and new Sec. 413 conflict-of-interest rulemaking due 360 days after enactment
New "end user distribution" staking provisions: self-staking, self-custodial third-party staking, and custodial/ancillary staking, with a CFTC rule due 270 days after enactment
Anti-evasion clause makes it unlawful to knowingly evade "digital commodity issuer" classification, including via transfer of related intellectual property
New Sec. 110 applies the Bank Secrecy Act to digital commodity brokers, dealers, and direct-access exchanges; new Sec. 111 preserves Office of Government Ethics rules
Provisional-status regime added: registrants enter provisional status until 270 days after the final CFTC rulemakings, with annual maintenance fees
modified: Stablecoin definitions now cross-reference the GENIUS Act: "permitted payment stablecoin" and "permitted payment stablecoin issuer" defined by reference rather than spelled out
Affiliated-person sales cap rewritten — the fixed 8%/25% holding-resale limits replaced with percentages set by Commission rule (floor of 5 percent), via a rulemaking due 270 days after enactment
Prior-issuer reporting cut-over dates (January 1, 2020 / June 1, 2025) replaced with maturity-based and 4-year-clock disclosure rules tied to Securities Act Sec. 4B

Title III Sec. 304 changed from "Operation of Alternative Trading Systems" to "Rulemaking for Dual-Registered Entities," centered on conflict-of-interest policies and dual SEC/CFTC registration under new SEC Act Sec. 15(p)
Foreign-adversary studies expanded and renumbered to Sec. 511 within an enlarged Title V study slate (blockchain payments, illicit use, foreign-located intermediaries)
Common-control test broadened to also cover persons "acting pursuant to an agreement to act in concert"
Title becomes a dual-citation Act: "CLARITY Act of 2025" and the "Anti-CBDC Surveillance State Act"
removed: Deleted former Sec. 5k exemption (Sec. 411) for ATSs and registered intermediaries with caps (25% / $50,000,000,000 volume; 10% / $100,000,000 revenue)
Removed former Sec. 502 "Modernization of the SEC mission" inserting "innovation" into the SEC's efficiency mandate across four securities Acts
Removed the prior international-cooperation directive (old Sec. 109) for coordinating with foreign regulators
